_comment: OFF THE BALL, the podcast studio segment (docs/podcast.md; Tom's picks 2026-10-20: set B4, the booth over the ground; Tamsin Tregarrow on the left, Samir Haddani on the right; a new episode each regular-season day, Standard size). A DRAFT for Tom to read and edit: not loaded or validated by the channel yet, nothing voiced. As data/analyst.json: each kind has who says it (tamsin or samir), a gesture (talk, open, point: at the window's middle pane, laugh, nod, both), when it's said (the fact that makes it true, worked out by the build; none: always fits), its subject (team: the one team it names, voiced once per team), and ways, each a pair: say (spoken and typed in the bubble: fixed, or naming one team as {team}, spoken as studio.spokenTeam, 'the Gulls') and show (the middle pane's or the lower third's words, in capitals: any facts). No line says a player's name or '{team}'s'; numbers and players are on the pane. Tamsin: a former keeper from the Gullcoast, a career backup (Tom, 2026-10-20: most analysts were never the stars), sharp and dry, trusts her eyes; Samir teases her about the bench and she gets in first, poking fun at herself. Samir: a data analyst from Sunreach, quick and precise, enjoys being right. An episode: the opening, three or four topics dealt from the pool (each topic's kinds in its order, a kind skipped when its fact isn't true, a topic skipped when it has nothing true to say), PICKS, the close.

_themes: Tom (2026-10-20): after the hook (a topic tied to what's really going on), a longer discussion on its theme: scripted back-and-forth, sports talk in Scorchball's own terms, never naming a team or player, so it's true in any season and voiced once. Each theme lists the topics that lead into it (its hooks) and its discussions; an episode's discussion is the hook's theme's next one not yet aired (none repeats until the theme's four have all had a turn), the order seeded by the league. Batch 1 (2026-10-20): the kids and the title race; the other six themes to come (form, scoring and keeping, money, history, the fans, luck and judgement).
_discussions: Each a title for the window's middle pane and its lines in order (needs "poll": dealt only once a poll has opened, as it says there are polls; Tom, 2026-10-21), each line who says it, its gesture and what's said (one clip each, fixed). tag: a delivery tag for the voice (ElevenLabs v3, e.g. laughs, sighs), never shown in the bubble; used sparingly. The middle pane shows the title through the discussion and clears for its last few lines.

lines.say: So what actually makes a rookie work? Because some walk straight in and some just vanish.
The first five matches tell you a lot. The good ones touch the ball more each game. The others hide.
Hiding. That's exactly it. You can see it from the stands. They drift out to the touchline and wait.
And in this league you can't hide for long. Five a side, the ball finds you whether you like it or not.
My first start, I was terrified of the first cross. Mind you, it was my only start that season.
Well, here's the good news. I'd bet a rookie's second half of the season usually beats their first.
Of course it is. They've stopped thinking and started playing.
The rookie rule helps too. Every team has to start one, so nobody gets to sit them on the bench all year.
Some managers would, believe me. Lock them in the dugout with a clipboard.
And then they'd never learn. You learn the heat by playing in it. Nobody can teach you when to let go of the ball.
The burns. Every rookie burns it early. Holds it too long, looks up, and it's gone.
I want to count that one day. I bet rookies burn it far more in their first few weeks.
So be patient with them. That's my advice to every fan watching.
Patient, yes. But keep an eye on the touches. The numbers usually know first.
How much does an old head in the squad help a rookie? Genuinely, I'd love to know.
More than any number you've got. A good veteran talks the whole match. Where to stand, when to go.
I'll take that as a challenge. I'm sure there's a way to measure talking.
There isn't. I sat beside our first-choice keeper for six seasons. Best coaching I ever had, and none of it on the pitch.
Fine. My guess is rookies in front of an experienced keeper make fewer silly mistakes.
Because the keeper sees everything. The keeper is the one shouting.
There's another side, though. The veterans are the expensive ones. Under the cap, you can't keep them all.
That's the hard part. Do you pay the old pro, or give the minutes to the kid who'll be better next year?
The smart clubs do both. One veteran per line of the team, and the youngsters around them.
And the veteran has to want it. Some are happy to teach. Some just want the ball.
You can usually tell which by the assists. The teachers pass to the rookies. The others don't look.
See, that one I believe. I've sat on the bench next to both kinds.
So a rookie's best friend is a generous veteran.
And a keeper who never stops talking. Write that down.
Let's talk about the draft. Because to me it's a lottery, in every sense.
Well, the order is a lottery for the teams that miss the playoffs. After that, it's judgement.
Judgement on an eighteen-year-old you've seen play a handful of times.
That's why the scouting matters. The reports are never quite right. Some kids are better than they look.
And some look great in a highlight and then can't do it on a wet Tuesday.
There are usually two big names each year. The first pick tends to be good straight away.
Tends to be. But the best players I've seen weren't always the first names called.
That's fair. Potential takes years to show. Some players peak late, around twenty-eight, twenty-nine.
So what should a team draft? The best player, or what they need?
The best player, nearly always. Needs change. A good player is good wherever you put them.
Unless you draft three keepers. Ask me what it's like being the third one.
I've seen the photos. Lovely tracksuit, though.
Honestly, the draft is the most exciting night of the off-season. All that hope.
Hope, and a lot of spreadsheets. For me, anyway.
Can we spare a minute for the Kindling League? It doesn't get talked about enough.
The reserves. Where the draft picks go when they don't make the squad.
Exactly. Ten in a squad, and anyone who doesn't fit plays there instead. Out of sight.
It's a tough place to be. You were drafted, everyone was excited, and then you're playing in front of nobody.
But it's not a dead end. A call-up can come any time there's a gap in the squad.
And when it comes you have to be ready that day. Not next week. That day.
Some of them come up better than they went down. A season of playing every week helps.
Playing every week is everything. You don't get better watching from the bench.
Says the backup keeper. You sat on the bench for whole seasons.
That's why I'm so wise. I had a lot of time to think.
Seriously, though, it's a good system. Nobody's career ends just because the squad was full.
And for the fans, it's a reason to watch the call-ups. Every one has a story.
The kid nobody talked about, suddenly starting a big match.
That's sport. That's why we love it.

racePressure.title: THE TITLE RACE · PRESSURE AT THE TOP

lines.say: Is it harder to lead the table or to chase it? I go back and forth on this.
Leading. Every time. When you're chasing, you've got nothing to lose.
I'm not so sure. Leaders hold on more often than people think.
Hold on, maybe. But look at their faces. Every match feels like a final.
That's fair. I'd bet the pressure shows in the late goals, when it's tight.
Because they're defending a lead in their heads before they've even got one.
And with three points for a win, one bad afternoon and you're caught.
A draw feels like a defeat when you're top. A draw feels like a win when you're chasing.
Same point, different feelings. I love that. It drives the model mad.
The model doesn't have a stomach. The players do.
So what does a leader do? How do you play top of the table?
You play the same way that got you there. The moment you change, they smell it.
I'll give you that. The teams that sit back usually get punished.
Keep attacking. Keep the ball hot. Let them worry about you.

raceRun.title: THE TITLE RACE · HOW A RUN STARTS

lines.say: Every title team has a run somewhere. Five, six wins on the bounce. Where does it come from?
Usually a scrappy win. Not a pretty one. A win they didn't deserve.
The lucky ones. Ugly goal in the last minute, and suddenly they believe.
Belief is hard to measure, but you can see it after. The shots go up, the burns go down.
Because they stop panicking with the ball. They know a chance is coming.
And momentum helps in the moment. A scorcher, and they're on top for the next minute and a half.
You can hear it in the crowd. The whole ground leans forward.
But a run ends. They all do. The question is how they handle the first defeat.
The good teams lose one and then win the next. The others lose two, then three.
The bounce back is the stat I watch. It says more about a team than the run itself.
Character. That's what you're measuring, whether you like the word or not.
I'll call it a bounce-back rate, and you can call it character.
Either way, when a team starts winning ugly, watch out.
That's the one thing we agree on today.

raceLastRound.title: THE TITLE RACE · THE LAST ROUND

lines.say: Let's talk about the last round. All the matches at once. It's chaos.
The best night of the season. The table changes every time someone scores.
The top four go through, so the fight for fourth can be the best story of the night.
And the players know the scores elsewhere. You can't stop the crowd telling them.
That changes how they play. A team that only needs a draw starts sitting deeper.
And then concedes in the last minute. I've seen it a hundred times, from the best seat in the house. The bench.
You keep saying a hundred. The league hasn't had a hundred last rounds.
It's a figure of speech, Samir. It feels like a hundred.
What I like is that nobody can rest anyone. Every point is real, right to the end.
For the teams already out, it's pride. And they love spoiling someone's night.
Teams with nothing to play for often do better than you'd expect. Free legs.
No pressure, no fear. That's when players are at their best.
So tune in for all of it. Flick between the grounds.
And don't blink. It's over in twenty minutes a half.
Here's one for you. Does the Pennant actually matter, or is it all about the Cup?
It matters to me. Top of the table after a whole regular season. That's the best team, over time.
Over time, maybe. But nobody remembers who won the Pennant. They remember who lifted the Cup.
That's a shame, because the Pennant is the fairer prize. The Cup is two matches. Anything can happen.
That's the beauty of it. Two matches, and the best team can still lose.
It's a beauty if you're the underdog. Ask the team that topped the table and went out in the semifinal.
Then they should have won the semifinal. That's the job.
One bad half, a golden goal, a shootout. It's harsh.
Harsh is what makes it exciting. If the best team always won, why would anyone watch?
I'll admit, finishing top does help. The top seed plays the fourth, and plays at home.
Home matters in a semifinal. The noise alone is worth a goal.
So the Pennant buys you a better path to the Cup. That's what it's worth.
Win both, and nobody can argue.
Win both, and I'll stop arguing. For a day.
Old question. Form or class? A hot team, or the team that's just better?
Form, over a week. Class, over a season. Over one match, I'll take form every time.
I'm not sure form is even real. Five results is a tiny sample. Flip a coin five times.
Flip a coin. Tell that to a team that's lost four in a row.
I'm serious. A good team with bad luck looks out of form. Then it turns, and everyone calls it a revival.
Some of it's luck, fine. But you can see a team that's sure of itself. They pass quicker. They want the ball.
That I'll accept. Fewer burns, more shots. The ball moves before it gets too hot.
And class shows when things go wrong. A good side goes a goal down and doesn't panic.
Class is the goal difference. Form is the last five letters on the graphic.
Lovely. Put that on a mug.
I might. Off the Ball merchandise. Somebody has to fund the coffee.
So in a big match, who do you back? The hot side, or the good side?
The good side. Every time. Form fades. Class stays.
And I'd back the hot side. So one of us is right this week.
Let's talk about confidence. Because you can't put it in a spreadsheet, Samir.
Watch me. Shots from outside the arc. Confident players shoot from further out.
Fair, actually. A striker with no confidence passes when they should shoot.
Or holds it, waiting for the perfect chance, and the ball burns at their feet.
Keepers are the same. A confident keeper comes off their line. A nervous one stays rooted.
And you? Were you a come-off-your-line keeper?
I was a come-off-the-bench keeper. Very different skill. Mostly stretching.
That's the most honest thing anyone's said on this show.
Seriously, though, it's fragile. One mistake in front of the home crowd, and it's gone for weeks.
And it comes back the same way. One good moment. A scorcher, a big save.
That's why managers keep picking a struggling player. They're waiting for that one moment.
Or they've got nobody else. That happens too.
Trust me, I know. Nobody else is how I got all three of my starts.
Three starts. I'll look them up. For research.
How does a team get out of a bad run? Because some never do, and some are fine a week later.
Simple things. Keep the ball, take fewer risks, get a clean sheet. Then build.
I'd bet the opposite, actually. Teams in a bad run hold the ball too long.
Because they're scared to lose it. And then they burn it anyway.
Exactly. The heat doesn't care how nervous you are. Forty seconds and it's gone.
So what would you do, coach Samir?
Coach Samir. I like that. Move the ball early. Shoot more. Make the other team do the worrying.
That's brave. When you're losing, nobody wants to be the one who shoots and misses.
That's the trap. Everybody hides, nobody shoots, and the run gets longer.
It's the dressing room too. A bad run is quiet. Nobody's talking.
Who breaks the silence? The captain?
Usually the backup keeper with a terrible joke. It was my one job for years.
So the secret to ending a losing run is a bad joke from the bench.
Don't laugh. It's worked more than once.
Momentum. Everyone says it in every sport. But here it's actually a thing, isn't it?
It is. A scorcher, or the other team burning the ball, and you get it for a minute and a half.
And you can feel it. The players with momentum just look sharper.
They are sharper. That's the point. It's a real lift while it lasts.
What surprised me is how often it comes from burns. The other team gives it to you.
Most of it does. About two in every three times. You earn it by making them hold the ball.
So defending well is how you attack. Press them, make them wait, let the ball burn.
And then pounce in that minute and a half. The best teams know exactly when they've got it.
And it doesn't stack. Score another scorcher and it just starts again.
Which stops runaway games. The other side can take it straight back.
I'd have loved momentum. Mind you, I'd have needed to be on the pitch.
You'd have had bench momentum. A really good minute and a half of sitting.
Elite sitting. Ask anyone who played with me.
Next time momentum swings, watch the press. That's where it starts.
The scorcher. The thing that makes this sport different. Why do they go in so often?
Because by then the ball is red hot and moving like nothing else. A keeper barely sees it.
But you have to keep the ball long enough to get it hot. That's the risk.
Too long and it burns. Too short and it's just a normal shot. It's all about the timing.
It's the best gamble in sport. Hold it, hold it, and either it's a scorcher or you've given it away.
As a keeper, you know when it's coming. The crowd tells you. They get louder and louder.
And you'd know that from the bench, would you?
The bench is very close to the crowd, Samir. I heard everything.
The best scorers are patient. They let the team build it and arrive at the right moment.
And they shoot first time. No touch. A touch is a moment wasted.
A scorcher gives your team momentum too. So it's worth more than a goal.
And for the keeper, it's the one goal nobody blames you for.
Unless you'd stepped off your line to wave at the crowd.
That was one time, and it was a lovely wave.
Right, I have to talk about keepers. It's the loneliest job in sport.
Lonelier than the backup keeper?
No, fine, that's lonelier. The backup is lonely and cold.
It's a strange job, though. The first-choice keeper only comes off if they're injured.
So the backup gets one or two starts a season. If that. You live on hope and stretching.
What makes a great keeper? I'll say save percentage, and you'll say something else.
Nerve. Concentration. You might not touch the ball for minutes, then you have to be perfect.
